 Readers push back on a sleep scientist’s case for permanent standard time.
 Print this Article 
 View Comments Morning commuters waited for the train in Maplewood, N.J., in February. Daylight saving time means later sunsets, but at the cost of darker mornings. DAVE SANDERS/NYT The op-ed by Susan Kohl Malone (“ Permanent daylight saving time is not the fix we think it is ,” Opinion, Oct. 19) argues against making daylight saving time permanent by underscoring its impact on circadian rhythms. 
 At least three arguments complicate the notion that clock time needs to align with daylight time. 
 First, the position of the sun in the sky varies by an hour or more between the easternmost and westernmost points of each time zone in the United States. For example, on Oct. 19, the sun sets in Lexington, Ky., at 6:54 p.m. and in Boston at 5:56 p.m. It’s not entirely clear that the additional hour of daylight in Kentucky has any demonstrable effects on the health of Lexington residents as compared to their counterparts in Boston. 
 Second, as Malone points out, clock time does not change the actual amount of daylight in a day. Yet in much of the United States, day length varies so much over the year that our sleep-wake cycles cannot be aligned with it. In Boston, the longest day is 15 hours and 17 minutes and the shortest is 9 hours and 4 minutes, a difference of 6 hours and 13 minutes. Which of these is our circadian rhythm aligned with? 
 Get College Town A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns. Enter Email Sign Up Finally, even if the body’s circadian rhythm adjusts gradually as days grow shorter or longer, suddenly changing the clock by an hour allows for no such gradual adjustment. 
 Karl Kuban 
 Plymouth 
 3:32 a.m. That’s when the sky would start to lighten next June in Boston if we adopted year-round Eastern Standard Time. 
 Susan Kohl Malone‘s op-ed offers a one-size-fits-all solution for picking the best time for setting our clocks year-round. She wants us to use the time that currently holds sway for only about four months — early November through mid-March — all year. 
 Massachusetts already put together a commission , of which I was a member , to study the issue. We determined that the Commonwealth plus its neighboring states would be best served by Atlantic Standard Time, which is the same as Eastern Daylight Time year-round. Senate President Karen Spilka endorsed the approach this past March. 
 Additionally, as the Globe’s Dave Epstein has noted , low-angle morning light is important for setting our internal clocks — and with a 4 a.m. sunrise, most of us would sleep right through it. 
 Let the Midwest pick its own destiny, whether it’s the time they use in the winter or the summer. Here in New England we deserve to be on the best time that works for us, which is Atlantic Standard Time. 
 Tom Emswiler 
 Quincy
